meaning: to give back; to return (something borrowed); to pay back

senses.en: to give back; to return something borrowed (a book, a phone)
to pay back: 还 + person + 钱 (还我钱 'pay me back')

examples.en: Can you pay me back tomorrow?
examples.analysis: 还 takes two objects here, the person first and then the thing: 还 + 我 + 钱 'give me back the money'. 能…吗 turns the sentence into a polite 'can you…?' question.

examples.en: I'll take these books back tomorrow.
examples.analysis: The thing being returned, 这些书, is put first as the topic, so 还 ends the sentence with nothing after it. 去 + 还 = 'go and return': 去 before a verb says you go somewhere to do it.

examples.zh: 上次的钱你还没还我呢。
examples.en: You still haven't paid me back the money from last time.
examples.analysis: The same character twice, with two readings: the first, hái, means 'still' (a separate entry); the second, huán, is this verb. 没 + 还 = 'haven't paid back'. 呢 at the end stresses that this is still the situation.

collocations.en: to give back to (还给你 'here, I'm giving it back to you')

related.en: still; also; even more (a different reading, separate entry)
to borrow; to lend (the step before 还)

meaning: on; on top of; to go up; to go to; last (上次 'last time')

senses.en: on; on top of, after a noun (桌子上 'on the table')
to go up; to get on; to go to (上二楼, 上车, 上班, 上哪儿去？)
last; previous, before a time word (上次 'last time', 上个月 'last month')

examples.en: Your phone is on the table.
examples.analysis: 上 after a noun turns it into a place: 桌子上 'on the table'. The pattern is thing + 在 + noun + 上. English puts 'on' before 'the table'; Chinese puts 上 after 桌子.

examples.en: Let's go up to the second floor to eat.
examples.analysis: Here 上 is a verb, 'go up to', and the floor follows it directly: 上二楼, with no word for 'to'. The second verb, 吃饭, says what you go up for; 吧 makes the whole thing a suggestion.

examples.en: Where are you off to?
examples.analysis: In casual northern speech 上 + a place can mean 'go to', especially in questions like 上哪儿(去)？ 你上哪儿去 is a friendly 'where are you headed?'. 去 at the end repeats the idea of going. 你去哪儿？ asks the same in a neutral way that works everywhere.

collocations.en: to go to work; to be at work
to go to class; class starts
to get on (a bus, a train, into a car)

related.en: below; under; to go down; to get off
on top; above; the upper side

meaning: you (plural); you all; you guys

senses.en: you, speaking to two or more people (subject or object)
your, before a group or place you belong to (你们学校 'your school')

examples.en: Where are you guys going?
examples.analysis: 你们 is the subject, 'you' for a group. The question word stands where the answer will go: 你们去哪儿 'you go where?', answered 我们去北京. There is no 吗: 哪儿 already makes it a question, so a question like this does not take 吗.

examples.en: Today I'm treating you all to a meal.
examples.analysis: 你们 is the object of 请 'invite, treat' and also the people who will eat: 请 + person + 吃饭 = 'treat someone to a meal'. Said like this, it tells everyone the speaker is paying.

examples.en: Are you all doctors?
examples.analysis: 都 'all' before the verb takes in every person in 你们: 你们都是医生 'you are all doctors'. 吗 at the end turns the statement into a yes/no question.

meaning: to pass; to go past; to cross; to spend (a birthday, a holiday)

senses.en: to pass; to go past or across (过路口, 过马路)
to spend; to celebrate (a birthday, New Year)
(of time) to pass: 过两天 'in a couple of days'

examples.zh: 过了路口，医院就在右边。
examples.en: Once you're past the intersection, the hospital is on the right.
examples.analysis: 过 is 'go past': 过了路口 'having passed the intersection'. 了 marks the passing as done, and 就 'then, right' ties the second half to it: once you are past, the hospital is right there on the right. Typical when giving directions or guiding a taxi driver.

examples.en: How do you want to spend your birthday?
examples.analysis: 过 + an occasion = 'spend, celebrate': 过生日, 过年. Here the occasion, 生日, comes first as the topic, and 怎么 'how' sits right before 过.

examples.en: We'll come and see you in a couple of days.
examples.analysis: 过 + a stretch of time = 'once that time has passed': 过两天 'in a couple of days', often loose rather than exactly two. Like other time words it goes before the verb: at the front, as here, or after the subject (我们过两天去看你).

related.en: after a verb: have done before (去过); a separate entry, HSK 2
to arrive at; to reach (过 goes past it)

meaning: to not have; there is no; did not, have not (done)

senses.en: to not have; there isn't / aren't (the negative of 有)
did not; have not: negates an action that didn't happen (没有去)

examples.en: I don't have time today.
examples.analysis: 没有 is the negative of 有 'have': 我有时间 becomes 我没有时间. 有 is negated with 没, not 不; 不有 is not said.

examples.en: We're out of milk at home.
examples.analysis: With a place first, 没有 means 'there is no': 家里没有牛奶 'there's no milk at home'. 了 at the end marks a change, so it means 'we've run out', not 'we never keep any'.

examples.en: Have you eaten yet?
examples.analysis: 没有 at the end asks 'or not?' about an action: 吃饭了没有 'have you eaten or not?'. Answer 吃了 'I have' or 还没有 'not yet'. Around mealtimes a question like 吃了吗？ also works as a friendly hello.

related.en: short form of 没有 in speech (没时间, 没去)
negates the present and future, habits, wishes and adjectives (不去, 不忙); 没有 negates having and actions that did not happen

meaning: to look; to watch; to read; to visit; to think (我看…)

senses.en: to look at; to watch; to read (看电视, 看书)
to visit; to go and see someone (看朋友)
to think, judge: 我看… 'I think…; I guess…'

examples.en: Look, it's raining!
examples.analysis: 你看 on its own, before a pause, calls someone's attention: 'look!'. In 下雨了, 了 marks the change from dry weather to rain: 'it has started raining'.

examples.en: Let's go and see Grandma tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 看 + a person = 'visit, go and see': 去看奶奶. 去 before 看 says you travel there to do it, and 吧 at the end turns the plan into a suggestion.

examples.en: I guess he's not coming today.
examples.analysis: 我看 + a whole clause = 'I think / I guess…', a casual way to give an opinion or a guess, not necessarily about something you saw. In 不来了, 了 marks a change: he was expected, but now it seems he won't come.

collocations.en: to see a doctor; (of a doctor) to see patients

related.en: to see; to catch sight of (look and actually see)
to see; to get to see

meaning: really; truly; so (before an adjective); real, true

senses.en: so; really, as an exclamation about a quality (真好, 真热)
really, truly, before a verb or in a question (你真不去？)
real; genuine; true (mostly as 真的)

examples.en: It's so hot today!
examples.analysis: 真 + adjective is an exclamation, the speaker's own reaction: 真热 'so hot!'. For a calm, neutral description, 很 is the usual choice: 今天很热.

examples.en: You're really not going?
examples.analysis: 真 before 不去 means 'really, truly': the speaker is surprised and checks. 了 marks a change of plan. There is no 吗; the rising voice alone makes it a question.

examples.en: I'm so sorry I'm late.
examples.analysis: 真 strengthens the apology: 真对不起 'really sorry'. In 来晚了, 晚 'late' comes after the verb to say how the coming turned out. A standard line when you arrive late.

collocations.en: really good; not bad at all

related.en: very; the neutral link before an adjective

meaning: particle after a verb: a continuing state or ongoing action (-ing)

senses.en: after a verb: a state that continues (门开着 'the door is open')
an action going on, often with 呢 (下着雨呢 'it's raining')
V1着 + V2: the manner of V2 (走着去 'go on foot')

examples.en: The door's open, come on in.
examples.analysis: 开 alone is the action 'to open'; 开着 is the state it leaves, the door standing open. 着 describes how things are at the moment, not the act itself. 进来吧 is a friendly 'come in'.

examples.en: Don't just stand there, have a seat!
examples.analysis: 站着 = 'standing (and staying that way)'. 别 + verb + 着 asks someone not to stay in that state. 请坐 'please sit' follows as the polite offer, a common line when a guest arrives.

examples.en: It's raining outside.
examples.analysis: 着 goes straight after the verb, so it splits 下雨 'to rain' into 下着雨. 呢 at the end adds 'as things stand right now'. 外边在下雨 says much the same with 在 before the verb.

related.en: before a verb: in the middle of doing (在下雨)
right now, in the middle of
marks a completed action or a change

meaning: matter; thing; business; something to do

senses.en: matter; thing; affair (这事 'this matter')
something to do; business; a problem (今天事多 'lots to do today')

measure.note: 一件事; casual speech also uses 个: 有个事

examples.en: There's something I want to ask you.
examples.analysis: 有个事 = 'have a matter': 一 is dropped, and the casual measure 个 stands in for the standard 件. The words after it, 想问你, say what the matter is: 'something I want to ask you'.

examples.en: Don't tell him about this.
examples.analysis: 这事 'this matter' comes first as the topic; in speech the measure word after 这 is often left out. Then 你别告诉他 is the request. English needs 'about this'; Chinese just puts 这事 in front.

examples.en: There's way too much to do today.
examples.analysis: Here 事 means 'things to do, tasks'. The time word comes first, 事 is the subject, and 太多了 'too many' is the comment. A common way to say you are swamped.

collocations.en: to be busy; to have something on

related.en: a thing you can touch; 事 is a matter or a task

meaning: how; how come, why (with surprise)

senses.en: how; in what way: 怎么 + verb (怎么说, 怎么去)
how come; why, with surprise or concern (你怎么不吃了？)

examples.en: How do you say this in Chinese?
examples.analysis: 怎么 + verb asks for the way to do it: 怎么说 'how to say'. 用汉语 'using Chinese' comes before it and names the means. Point at something and ask this whenever you lack a word.

examples.en: How come you haven't left work yet?
examples.analysis: Before a negative, 怎么 asks 'how come?' with surprise, not 'in what way'. 还没 'still not' + 下班 'finish work': the speaker expected the person to have gone home by now.

examples.en: Come here, I'll show you how to do it.
examples.analysis: 怎么 also works inside a statement: 教你怎么做 'teach you how to do it', where 怎么做 is the thing being taught. 来 at the start is a friendly 'come here'. Asked on its own, 怎么做？ means 'how do I do it?'.

collocations.en: which way?; how do I get there?

meaning: now; at the moment; these days

senses.en: now; right now; at the moment
nowadays; these days (现在的孩子 'kids these days')

examples.en: Where are you right now?
examples.analysis: 现在 is a time word, and time words go before the verb, not at the end as in English: 你 + 现在 + 在哪儿. Then 在 is the verb 'be at', and 哪儿 'where' sits where the answer will go.

examples.zh: 我现在很忙，晚上给你打电话。
examples.en: I'm busy right now; I'll call you this evening.
examples.analysis: 现在 sets the time of the first half and 晚上 the time of the second, each before its verb. Setting 'now' against 'later' like this is how people politely put off a call. 很 + adjective is the normal way to state a quality.

examples.en: He works in Shanghai now.
examples.analysis: 现在 here means 'these days, at this stage', not this very minute: his current job is in Shanghai. The order is time, then place (在上海), then the action (工作).

meaning: o'clock; to order (food); a dot, a point

senses.en: o'clock, an hour on the clock (八点 'eight o'clock')
to order (food, drinks); to pick from a list
dot; point; spot (also the 点 in 一点儿 'a little')

examples.zh: 我们八点在门口见，好吗？
examples.en: Let's meet at the entrance at eight, OK?
examples.analysis: Number + 点 = 'o'clock': 八点 'eight o'clock'. The time comes first, with no word for 'at' before it, then 在 + place (在门口 'at the entrance'), then the verb 见 'meet'. 好吗 at the end asks for agreement.

examples.en: I finish work at seven-thirty in the evening.
examples.analysis: 七点半 = 'half past seven': 半 'half' comes after 点. The larger unit goes first, 晚上 'evening', then 七点半, and all of it sits before the verb 下班.

examples.en: What would you like to order?
examples.analysis: Here 点 is a verb: 'to order' from a menu. 想 + 点 = 'want to order', and 什么 sits in the object slot. A waiter, or a friend handing you the menu, will ask this.

related.en: minute on the clock (八点十分 '8:10')
an hour as a length of time; 点 is a time on the clock

meaning: particle: 'what about…?'; 'where is…?'; still going on

senses.en: after a noun or pronoun: 'what about…?' (你呢？ 'and you?')
noun + 呢 when someone or something is missing: 'where is…?'
at the end of a statement: the situation is still going on (还在…呢)

examples.en: I'm a doctor. What about you?
examples.analysis: 你呢 turns the topic over to the listener: after 'I'm a doctor', it means 'and what do you do?'. Just the person + 呢, no verb. What it asks comes from what was just said.

examples.en: Where's Xiao Wang? Isn't he coming?
examples.analysis: When someone expected is missing, name + 呢 asks 'where is…?'. The follow-up 他不来吗 is a 吗 question, 'isn't he coming?'. After a different remark, the same 小王呢 could mean 'what about Xiao Wang?'.

examples.en: He's still asleep.
examples.analysis: Here 呢 at the end of a statement says the situation is still going on. It often pairs with 还 'still' and 在 'in the middle of': 还在睡觉呢 'still sleeping'. It adds the sense 'as things stand right now'.

related.en: turns a statement into a yes/no question; 呢 follows up or goes with a question word

meaning: don't (telling someone not to do something)

senses.en: don't…: tells someone not to do something (别走 'don't go')
别…了: stop…; don't… any more (别生气了, 别买了)

examples.en: Come on, don't be angry.
examples.analysis: 别 + verb tells someone not to do something. 了 at the end shows the person is already angry and is being asked to stop: 'don't be angry any more'. Without 了, 别生气 sounds more like 'don't get angry'.

examples.zh: 明天别忘了给我打电话。
examples.en: Don't forget to call me tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 别忘了 + action = 'don't forget to…', a set way to remind someone. Here 了 belongs with 忘 'forget'. What not to forget follows: 给我打电话 'call me'. The time word 明天 goes in front.

examples.en: Don't buy it, it's way too expensive!
examples.analysis: 别买了: the other person is about to buy, and the speaker says 'drop it'. The second 了 belongs to 太…了 'too…'. No word for 'it' is needed; the thing is clear from the situation.

collocations.en: don't stand on ceremony; you're welcome

related.en: don't (a little firmer; common on signs)

meaning: to walk; to leave, to go; to go (by a route)

senses.en: to walk; to go on foot
to leave; to set off (我先走了 'I'm off')
to go by a route: 怎么走？ 'which way?'

examples.en: It's not far, let's walk.
examples.analysis: 走 is 'walk' here. 走着去 = 'go walking', that is, on foot: the first verb with 着 says how the second one, 去, happens. 不远 'not far' gives the reason first, as Chinese often does.

examples.en: I'm heading off. Bye!
examples.analysis: 走 means 'leave' here, not 'walk'. 先 'first' says you leave before the others, so 我先走了 is the polite way to leave a meal, a meeting or the office. 了 marks the change about to happen.

examples.en: How do I get to the station?
examples.analysis: 怎么走 asks for the route: 'which way do I go?'. 去车站 'to the station' comes first, then 怎么走. Ask a passer-by this; to ask about the means (bus, taxi), people say 怎么去.

collocations.en: to walk; to go on foot

related.en: to go to a place; 走 is to walk or to leave

meaning: too; so (太…了); 不太: not very

senses.en: too, more than wanted (太贵了 'too expensive')
so, really, with delight (太好了 'great!')
不太 + adjective: not very (a soft negative)

examples.en: It's too expensive. I'm not getting it.
examples.analysis: 太 + adjective + 了 = 'too…': 太贵了 'too expensive'. In 不买了, 了 marks a change of mind: the speaker was going to buy it, and now won't.

examples.en: The food here is so good!
examples.analysis: With a good quality, 太…了 is praise, not a complaint: 太好吃了 'so delicious!'. Only the context tells 'too' from 'so': 太贵了 complains, 太好吃了 delights.

examples.en: I'm not very hungry.
examples.analysis: 不太 + adjective = 'not very', a softer no than plain 不饿 'not hungry'. People use it to turn down food politely or to soften bad news, as in 不太好 'not great'.

meaning: in; inside (after a noun: 车里, 房间里)

senses.en: in; inside, after a noun (书包里 'in the schoolbag')
the inside (里边 is the fuller form)

examples.en: Is your phone in the car?
examples.analysis: 里 after a noun turns it into a place: 车里 'in the car'. The pattern is thing + 在 + noun + 里, and 吗 makes it a yes/no question. English puts 'in' first; Chinese puts 里 after the noun.

examples.en: There's no money left in my wallet.
examples.analysis: Place + 没有 + thing = 'there is no… in…': 钱包里 is the place, so it comes first. 了 marks the change: there was money, and now it is gone.

examples.en: It's too hot in the room.
examples.analysis: 房间里 'in the room' is the place being described, and 太热了 'too hot' is the comment. With country and city names like 中国 or 北京, 里 is not added: 在北京, not 在北京里.

meaning: with; and; (talk) to; the same as; to follow

senses.en: with; together with (跟朋友一起 'with friends'); informally also 'and' between two nouns (我跟他 'he and I')
to a listener (跟他说 'tell him'); compared with (跟你一样)
to follow (跟我来 'follow me')

examples.en: I'm going with friends tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 跟 + person + 一起 + verb = 'do it together with someone'. The whole phrase 跟朋友一起 goes before the verb 去, where English puts 'with friends' after 'going'.

examples.en: Have you told him about this?
examples.analysis: 跟 + person + 说 = 'say to, tell someone': the listener comes before the verb. 这事 'this matter' is the topic at the front, and 了吗 asks whether it has been done.

examples.en: I'm the same as you: I don't eat meat either.
examples.analysis: A 跟 B 一样 = 'A is the same as B'. Here it compares the speaker with the listener, and 也 'also' then says what they share: not eating meat.

related.en: and; with (more neutral; 跟 is more colloquial)

meaning: to tell; to let someone know

senses.en: to tell: 告诉 + person (+ the news)
to let someone know (告诉我 'let me know')

examples.en: Who told you?
examples.analysis: 告诉 is followed by the person told: 告诉你. The 的 at the end asks about a detail of something that has already happened, here the source of the news.

examples.en: Whatever you feel like eating, just tell me.
examples.analysis: 告诉 + 我 = 'tell me'. Here 什么 means 'whatever', not 'what?', and 就 links the two halves: 'if there is something you want to eat, then tell me'. A typical thing for a host to say.

examples.en: Don't tell him I'm here.
examples.analysis: 告诉 can take two objects: first the person (他), then the news (我在这儿 'I'm here'), with no word for 'that' in between. 别 at the front turns it into a request not to.

related.en: to say; to speak (跟他说); 告诉 usually takes the person as its object

meaning: again (in the future); then, only after that; later

senses.en: again; once more, for something not yet done (再给我…)
then; only after that (A 了再 B: first A, then B)
later; put off until then (明天再去 'go tomorrow instead')

examples.en: Another glass of water, please.
examples.analysis: 再 + verb = 'again, one more time', for something that has not happened yet: 再给我 'give me again'. With 一杯水 it comes out as 'another glass of water'. 请 at the front makes it polite.

examples.en: Have something to eat before you go.
examples.analysis: A 了 + 再 + B = 'do A first, then B': eat, then leave. Here 再 means 'only then', not 'again'. Hosts say this to a guest who is getting up to leave.

examples.zh: 今天太晚了，明天再去吧。
examples.en: It's too late today. Let's go tomorrow instead.
examples.analysis: 明天再 + verb = 'leave it until tomorrow': 再 marks a later time, not a repeat. 再 fits because the going has not happened yet; for an 'again' that already happened, speakers normally use 又.

collocations.en: let's talk about it later; besides

related.en: again, for something that has already happened
